title: AI Agents That Matter
author: Sayash Kapoor · Benedikt Stroebl · Zachary S. Siegel · Nitya Nadgir · Arvind Narayanan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The supplied excerpts are bibliography entries only. Although they cite work on benchmark inadequacies, reproducibility, interaction-based evaluation, risks and governance, they do not reveal whether AI Agents That Matter endorses, rejects or materially develops the cluster’s proposition that benchmark scores may lack workplace meaning.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The EntityClusterSummary contains no title, description, key points, or quotations, so there is no source evidence from which to assess a position relative to the cluster synthesis.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The supplied material is only bibliography and does not reveal the source’s own argument or findings. Although cited titles concern reproducible evaluation and limits of self-correction, citations alone cannot establish whether the source supports the cluster’s proposition.
qs: Lessons from the Trenches on Reproducible Evaluation of Lan-      guage Models, May 2024.

st.t: Agent benchmarks: Protocol scores are not competence
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that protocol scores alone do not establish real-world agent competence, and materially develops it through reproduction studies and concrete recommendations on reproducibility, cost controls, hold-outs, environmental effects and human-in-the-loop evaluation. It does not address automated-judge validity directly, but provides much of the empirical basis for the cluster’s broader methodological position.
qs: Without reproducible agent evaluation, it is hard to distinguish genuine improvements in agent designs from artifacts of the differences in evaluation choices.
Therefore, agent evaluations must be cost-controlled; otherwise it will     encourage researchers to develop extremely costly agents just to claim they topped the leaderboard.

st.t: Evaluation design: Preferences differ from professional correctness
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core premise that evaluation must match the system and task being assessed, and materially develops it for agents by distinguishing model from downstream evaluation and prescribing cost controls, hold-outs and standardization. It does not directly address human preference versus expert professional correctness, so its contribution is strongest on agent-specific evaluation design.
qs: Our thesis is that agents are sufficiently different from models that benchmarking practices need to be rethought.

We have taken the first steps toward a principled approach to agent benchmarking, resulting in recommendations including cost-controlled comparisons, separating model and downstream evaluation, preventing shortcuts using appropriate hold-outs, and greater standardization of evaluation practices.

st.t: Evaluation validity: Benchmark safeguards impose trade-offs
st.an: The source accepts that benchmark results are bounded and safeguard-dependent, and materially develops the cluster’s contamination-control argument by identifying agent-specific overfitting risks, advocating held-out and potentially secret test sets, and tying acceptable specialisation to the agent’s intended scope.
qs: If a benchmark allows shortcuts, accuracy on the benchmark does not translate to the real world [32, 33, 52].
In addition to creating a test set, benchmark developers should consider keeping it secret to prevent LLM contamination or agent overfitting.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s view that benchmark performance does not establish real-world competence or value and materially extends it with an agent-specific evaluation framework. It adds cost-controlled comparisons, matched hold-outs, reproducibility standards and human-in-the-loop testing that accounts for user skill—concrete methods for making deployment evaluation use-context specific.
qs: Our thesis is that agents are sufficiently different from models that benchmarking practices need to be rethought.
The agent’s accuracy will depend not just on the system but also on the skill level of humans interacting with it.

kp.k: Agent benchmarking needs distinct standards from model evaluation
kp.d: Kapoor and colleagues argue that agent evaluations inadequately measure real-world usefulness because they prioritize accuracy, conflate model research with downstream procurement, permit benchmark shortcuts, and lack reproducibility. Their evidence concerns programming, question answering and web interaction rather than legal services. They recommend cost-controlled comparisons, appropriate holdouts and standardized evaluation.
qs: Our thesis is that agents are sufficiently different from models that benchmarking practices need to be rethought.
The overarching goal of our work is to stimulate the development of agents that are useful in the real world and not just accurate on benchmarks.

kp.k: Agency varies with autonomy, environment and system design
kp.d: The authors endorse treating agency as a spectrum rather than a binary category. Drawing on existing definitions, they identify environmental and goal complexity, natural-language instruction and reduced supervision, and design patterns including tool use, planning and dynamically controlled workflows as factors making systems more agentic.
qs: Many of them view it as a spectrum — sometimes denoted by the term ‘agentic’ [38] — rather than a binary definition of an agent.
Systems whose control flow is driven by an LLM, and hence dynamic, are more agentic [57, 5].

kp.k: Accuracy gains can reflect spending rather than architectural advances
kp.d: The authors argue that repeated stochastic model calls can improve benchmark accuracy without demonstrating better agent design, particularly where example tests provide inexpensive correctness signals. They therefore recommend controlling cost even when the research objective is identifying architectural advances rather than economizing. Their retry baseline invokes a model up to five times at temperature zero; warming raises temperature across attempts; escalation switches to progressively more expensive models.
qs: Accuracy alone cannot identify progress because it can be improved by scientifically meaningless methods such as retrying.
This can still lead to success after the first trial since LLMs aren’t deterministic even at temperature zero.

kp.k: Simple coding baselines rival costly complex agents
kp.d: Across five runs on 164 HumanEval problems, using LDB's modified benchmark with example tests for every task, GPT-4 warming achieved mean accuracy of 93.2% at $2.45 total benchmark cost, compared with 93.3% at $6.36 for LDB using GPT-4 for generation and debugging, and 88.0% at $134.50 for LATS using GPT-4. Escalation achieved 85.0% at $0.27 versus 80.2% at $0.63 for LDB using GPT-3.5. These are historical API-cost measurements, not current prices or per-task costs; robustness checks with June 2023 model versions produced substantially similar conclusions.
qs: There is no significant accuracy difference between our warming strategy and the best-performing agent architecture.
We run each agent five times and report the mean accuracy and the mean total cost on the 164 HumanEval problems.
Meanwhile, the escalation strategy strictly improves accuracy while costing less than half of LDB (GPT-3.5).

kp.k: Reflection and debugging benefits remain unestablished on HumanEval
kp.d: The authors distinguish demonstrated accuracy gains from explanations attributing those gains to planning, reflection or debugging. They argue that inadequate comparisons against simple baselines leave the contribution of these 'System 2' techniques unresolved on code generation. They explicitly allow that such techniques may be useful on harder programming tasks such as SWE-bench; the findings do not establish their general uselessness.
qs: Based on our findings, the question of whether debugging, reflection, and other such “System 2” approaches [22] are useful for code generation remains open, in line with other recent findings [50, 18].
It is possible that System 2 techniques will be useful on harder programming tasks than those represented in HumanEval, such as SWE-bench [21].

kp.k: Joint optimization reduces inference costs with similar retrieval accuracy
kp.d: The authors modify DSPy using Optuna to jointly optimize accuracy and prompt-token costs through temperatures, few-shot example counts and selection, and formatting instructions. On HotPotQA, they use 100 training samples for optimization and 200 evaluation samples, measuring whether all ground-truth documents were retrieved rather than final-answer correctness. Across five evaluation runs, they report 53% lower variable cost for GPT-3.5 and 41% lower cost for Llama-3-70B with similar accuracy relative to default DSPy approaches. They present this as an illustrative starting point, and note that error bars exclude optimization and resampling variability.
qs: for GPT-3.5, joint optimization leads to 53% lower variable cost with similar accuracy compared to both default DSPy implementations.
Similarly, for Llama-3-70B, it leads to a 41% lower cost while maintaining accuracy.
Note that the error bars account for the in-sample variance on the test set and do not account for the variability induced during optimization and resampling.

kp.k: Upfront optimization can pay off through repeated deployment
kp.d: The paper distinguishes fixed optimization costs from variable inference costs and argues that greater upfront expenditure can reduce recurring costs by finding shorter prompts and efficient few-shot examples. Figure A6 places the break-even points at 1,332 inferences for Llama-3-70B and 1,275 for GPT-3.5 in the illustrated comparison. The authors expect variable costs to dominate at large deployment volumes, while acknowledging that changing prices can alter comparisons.
qs: By spending more upfront on the one-time optimization of agent design, we can reduce the variable cost of running an agent (e.g., by finding shorter prompts and few-shot examples while maintaining accuracy).
Precisely, the point of intersection is reached after 1332 (1275) inferences for Llama-3-70B (GPT-3.5).

kp.k: Procurement needs dollar costs, not model-size proxies
kp.d: The authors distinguish scientific model evaluation, where compute controls can isolate architectural or training improvements, from downstream engineering evaluation, where actual price relative to accuracy informs purchasing. They argue that active parameters and compute are misleading proxies for API buyers and recommend reporting input/output token counts alongside dollar costs so users can recalculate comparisons for changing providers and prices.
qs: Downstream evaluation is an engineering question that helps inform a procurement decision of which model or agent to use in a particular application.
Downstream developers don’t care about the number of active parameters when they’re using an API. They simply care about the dollar cost relative to accuracy.

In turn, downstream evaluations of agents should include input/output token counts in addition to dollar costs, so that anyone looking at the evaluation in the future can instantly recalculate the cost using current prices.

kp.k: Benchmark query patterns can misrepresent deployment economics
kp.d: The NovelQA case study contrasts asking all questions immediately after supplying a novel with the sequential questioning expected in an application. In one evaluation of the multiple-choice subset, GPT-4 with RAG scored 67.89% at $52.80 total cost, versus 67.81% at $99.80 for long context. Their modeled single-question comparison yields an approximately 21.86-fold long-context/RAG cost ratio, rather than the roughly twofold benchmark ratio. They ran this evaluation only once because of cost and acknowledge that NovelQA's batching is justifiable for its model-evaluation purpose.
qs: Specifically, we found that the two approaches are roughly equally accurate, with RAG costing more than 20 times less (Table A5).
But on NovelQA, RAG costs half as much (a tenfold overestimate).
Due to the high cost of running the evaluation, we only ran our evaluations once.

kp.k: Holdouts must match the intended scope of generalization
kp.d: The authors prescribe in-distribution sample holdouts for distribution-specific benchmarks, out-of-distribution samples for task-specific benchmarks, unseen tasks for domain-general benchmarks, and unseen domains for fully general benchmarks. Their survey of 17 benchmarks reports appropriate holdouts in 1/1, 3/6, 1/8 and 0/2 respectively; seven lack holdouts and any stated plans to add them. They caution that classification sometimes required their best guess and that their appropriateness assessment includes stated intentions to create suitable holdouts.
qs: We propose as a core principle that the more general the intended generality of the agent, the more the held-out set should differ from the training set, as detailed in Table 1.
Hence we count a holdout as appropriate if there actually exists a holdout at the appropriate level of generality or the benchmark designers indicate intent to create such a holdout.

kp.k: Hardcoded policies can inflate apparent real-world web capability
kp.d: WebArena contains 812 tasks across clones of six websites and two tools. The authors examine STeP's reported 35.8% accuracy and identify hardcoded task policies, including constructing Reddit profile URLs, that may fail when websites change. They argue that WebArena neither models drift nor holds out unseen web tasks. They distinguish this criticism of benchmark interpretation from STeP's legitimate objective of composing policies for fixed, previously known tasks; reduced performance under drift or unseen tasks is argued rather than measured in this case study.
qs: It turns out that STeP hardcodes policies to solve the specific tasks included in WebArena.
However, WebArena does not model drift.
Unfortunately, WebArena lacks a held-out test set for evaluating whether an agent can perform well on unseen web tasks.

kp.k: Human supervision changes usefulness and deserves direct evaluation
kp.d: The paper argues that benchmarks largely omit intermediate patterns of human assistance between chatbot answers and fully autonomous execution. These include checking outputs, steering the system, correcting errors and confirming consequential actions. As external evidence, it cites Shi and colleagues' finding that simple feedback increased GPT-4 performance from 0% to over 86% on challenging programming problems. The authors suggest that excluding human interaction can underestimate usefulness, while stressing that human-in-the-loop evaluation is costly and depends on user skill.
qs: Thus, the lack of human-in-the-loop evaluation of agents might lead us to underestimate their usefulness (whereas the lack of held-out test sets leads to overoptimism).
The agent’s accuracy will depend not just on the system but also on the skill level of humans interacting with it.

kp.k: Evaluation inconsistencies undermine reproducibility and exaggerate performance
kp.d: The authors identify incompatible scripts, repurposed model benchmarks, costly repeated runs, environment-dependent errors and implementation bugs as root causes. On HumanEval, Reflexion excludes three tasks missing example tests, LATS excludes those three plus another task, and LDB adds example tests. Reproduced LATS GPT-4 accuracy is 88.0%, versus 94.4% reported; incomplete testing accounts for a mean three-percentage-point discrepancy. On WebArena, rate limits affect 30/129 Reddit tasks for STeP, whose logs sometimes mark failed actions as successful. The authors emphasize benchmark standardization rather than attributing all discrepancies to developer mistakes.
qs: Without reproducible agent evaluation, it is hard to distinguish genuine improvements in agent designs from artifacts of the differences in evaluation choices.
For example, both LATS [65] and STeP [47] marked some incorrectly completed tasks as correct.
Note that insufficient standardization of the benchmark, rather than mistakes made by the agent developers, is a major contributing factor to many of the observed discrepancies.

kp.k: Expensive evaluations obstruct reliable uncertainty estimates
kp.d: The paper illustrates the expense of repeated benchmarking using SWE-bench's more than 2,000 tasks and SWE-Agent's $4-per-task limit: a complete run could exceed $8,000. The authors connect such costs to the rarity of error bars and difficulty interpreting performance variation. In their reproduction attempts, some reported agent scores exceeded the maximum of five runs, while some reported baselines fell below the minimum.
qs: Evaluating SWE-Agent on the entire benchmark could cost over USD 8,000 for a single evaluation run.
The high cost makes it infeasible to run evaluations multiple times, and perhaps as a result, agent evaluations are rarely accompanied by error bars.

kp.k: Cost findings exclude substantial deployment and societal costs
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that their findings depend on historical pricing and technological constraints, do not cover every task environment or agent design, and do not extensively analyze environmental impact, annotation labor or system maintenance. They propose that cost measurement could also inform safety evaluation by revealing the affordability of dangerous capabilities, but explicitly state that their work does not directly address agent safety risks.
qs: Finally, other types of costs, including environmental impact, human labor for data annotation, and maintenance costs of AI systems, have not been extensively analyzed.
By providing tools to assess the affordability of potentially dangerous capabilities, our research can help identify and anticipate safety concerns before they become widespread.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kapoor and co-authors argue that AI-agent progress and practical usefulness are misrepresented by accuracy-only benchmarks; cheaper designs, realistic deployment tests and human-in-the-loop evaluation can change assessments of which agents are useful.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about AI-agent development and benchmarking, not legal services. The authors claim that simple retry, warming and escalation strategies can match or outperform complex coding agents at substantially lower cost; consequently, existing comparisons do not establish that planning, reflection or debugging cause the reported gains. They demonstrate that jointly optimizing cost and accuracy can reduce inference costs without a substantial loss of retrieval accuracy. They also argue that model benchmarks can mislead downstream procurement: their NovelQA case study finds similar accuracy for retrieval-augmented generation and long-context processing, but substantially different costs under individual-question use. Inadequate holdouts, benchmark-specific shortcuts and inconsistent evaluation can inflate expectations of real-world agent capability. Conversely, omitting human feedback can underestimate practical usefulness. Their broader claims about improved accessibility and reduced deployment impacts are potential benefits, not measured societal outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence combines repeated benchmark experiments, a survey of 17 benchmarks, reproduction audits, a single-run NovelQA comparison and separately attributed research on human feedback.
pts.d: On the modified 164-task HumanEval benchmark, five-run means show GPT-4 warming achieving 93.2% accuracy at $2.45 total API cost, compared with LDB using GPT-4 at 93.3% and $6.36, and LATS using GPT-4 at 88.0% and $134.50. Robustness checks using June 2023 model versions produce substantially similar conclusions. On HotPotQA, the authors optimize using 100 training samples and evaluate on 200 samples, reporting five-run averages: joint optimization reduces variable cost by 53% for GPT-3.5 and 41% for Llama-3-70B with similar retrieval accuracy. NovelQA's multiple-choice comparison reports 67.89% accuracy for RAG and 67.81% for long-context processing; the approximately 21.86-fold single-question cost ratio is calculated for that usage scenario rather than measured through a full sequential-query experiment. Their survey identifies seven benchmarks with neither holdouts nor stated plans for them, and only five of 17 satisfying their appropriate-holdout standard. WebArena's STeP policies illustrate brittleness to website changes; reproduction audits identify inconsistent task subsets, incorrectly scored successes and environmental effects. The human-feedback example is evidence from Shi et al., cited by the authors, not their own experiment. They do not empirically measure employment, legal-service outcomes or societal accessibility.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern the agent systems, benchmarks and API prices examined in spring 2024; broader improvements are conditional expectations without a fixed delivery date.
pts.d: The source is the July 2024 first version. HumanEval costs use April 2024 prices, while HotPotQA and NovelQA costs use May 2024 prices; the discussion also includes a June 2024 provider-price comparison. Cost rankings depend on model versions, provider prices and deployment patterns. Retry strategies depend on available correctness signals, and passing example tests does not guarantee passing held-out evaluation tests. Findings about complex agent designs are limited to the tested tasks: the authors explicitly allow that System 2 techniques may help on harder programming problems such as SWE-bench. Joint optimization requires upfront expenditure; in their HotPotQA example, its total-cost advantage over default few-shot optimization emerges at approximately 1,275 GPT-3.5 inferences and 1,332 Llama-3-70B inferences. The NovelQA cost advantage depends on asking individual questions rather than batching all questions with the novel. Generalization claims require holdouts matched to the agent's intended generality and relevant distribution shifts. Human-in-the-loop results depend on users' skills. Environmental impact, annotation labor and maintenance costs are not extensively analyzed, so the cost findings are not comprehensive lifecycle savings estimates.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are downstream developers and procurers, agent researchers, benchmark designers and users interacting with agents.
pts.d: Downstream developers risk selecting unnecessarily expensive or brittle systems if they treat model leaderboards as deployment guidance; the authors recommend dollar costs and realistic application-specific testing. Agent researchers may misattribute improvements to architectural complexity and waste time attempting to reproduce inconsistent results. Benchmark designers and leaderboard aggregators are assigned responsibility for appropriate holdouts, standardized evaluation and comparable submissions. Users such as programmers, data analysts and question-answering application users may benefit from cheaper systems and from feedback-assisted workflows, but their supervision and skill affect performance. The paper treats autonomy as a spectrum rather than assuming complete substitution of humans. Developers and deployers also face safety responsibilities: lower costs can make potentially dangerous capabilities more affordable. No specific claim is made about lawyers, law firms, legal clients or legal employment.
